techniques.name: Homomorphic Encryption
techniques.description: Homomorphic encryption lets a server compute on data that stays encrypted, so the server never sees the underlying values. The data owner encrypts the inputs, the server performs the arithmetic directly on the encrypted data, and only the holder of the secret key can decrypt the result. For machine learning, the model is first rewritten using operations the scheme supports, such as additions, multiplications and polynomial approximations of other functions. Exact schemes return the same answer as the unencrypted computation, while approximate schemes, often used for neural networks, return a close one. The guarantee is confidentiality of the data while it is processed, on the usual assumption that the server follows the protocol.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital group wants a cloud service to score patients' readmission risk without the provider seeing patient records. The hospital encrypts the patient features, the cloud evaluates a logistic regression model on the encrypted values, and the hospital decrypts the scores. A linear model is chosen on purpose, since encrypted computation becomes costly as models get larger.

A bank outsources credit scoring to a third-party cloud host. It encrypts customer financial data under a key that never leaves the bank, so an attacker who breaches the host, or an administrator there, can only copy ciphertexts. The bank checks that the host holds no decryption key and that the chosen parameters meet its required security level.

A research team outsources a genome-wide association study to a cloud server. The team encrypts participants' genotype and phenotype data, the server computes the association statistics on the ciphertexts, and only the final statistics are decrypted. One published prototype handled 1,000 individuals and 131,071 genetic variants in about ten minutes on a 28-core server.

limitations.description: Computation is typically orders of magnitude slower than on unencrypted data and ciphertexts are much larger, so real-time use, large models and large datasets are often out of reach. A published encrypted logistic regression training run took about 116 minutes on a real-world dataset.

Only some computations are practical. Circuit depth is limited by noise growth unless costly bootstrapping resets it, and comparisons and non-polynomial functions, such as most neural-network activations, must be approximated or quantised to integers, which can lower accuracy compared with the unencrypted model.

The usual security model is an honest-but-curious server. Ciphertexts can be altered, so encryption alone gives no assurance that the server ran the intended computation correctly, and a malicious host could return a wrong result that still decrypts without error.

Encryption protects data during processing, not what the result reveals. Whoever decrypts the output can still learn about the model or the data behind it through attacks such as membership inference, and with the approximate CKKS scheme, sharing decrypted results can enable a key-recovery attack.

Correct use needs cryptographic expertise. Choosing scheme parameters, encodings and noise budgets wrongly can leave the system insecure or stop results decrypting correctly, and the right choices differ by scheme and library.

resources.title: Fully homomorphic encryption using ideal lattices
resources.abstract: We propose a fully homomorphic encryption scheme -- i.e., a scheme that allows one to evaluate circuits over encrypted data without being able to decrypt. Our solution comes in three steps. First, we provide a general result -- that, to construct an encryption scheme that permits evaluation of arbitrary circuits, it suffices to construct an encryption scheme that can evaluate (slightly augmented versions of) its own decryption circuit; we call a scheme that can evaluate its (augmented) decryption circuit bootstrappable.

resources.title: Secure Logistic Regression Based on Homomorphic Encryption: Design and Evaluation
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND: Learning a model without accessing raw data has been an intriguing idea to security and machine learning researchers for years. In an ideal setting, we want to encrypt sensitive data to store them on a commercial cloud and run certain analyses without ever decrypting the data to preserve privacy. Homomorphic encryption technique is a promising candidate for secure data outsourcing, but it is a very challenging task to support real-world machine learning tasks. Existing frameworks can only handle simplified cases with low-degree polynomials such as linear means classifier and linear discriminative analysis. OBJECTIVE: The goal of this study is to provide a practical support to the mainstream learning models (eg, logistic regression). METHODS: We adapted a novel homomorphic encryption scheme optimized for real numbers computation. We devised (1) the least squares approximation of the logistic function for accuracy and efficiency (ie, reduce computation cost) and (2) new packing and parallelization techniques. RESULTS: Using real-world datasets, we evaluated the performance of our model and demonstrated its feasibility in speed and memory consumption. For example, it took approximately 116 minutes to obtain the training model from the homomorphically encrypted Edinburgh dataset. In addition, it gives fairly accurate predictions on the testing dataset. CONCLUSIONS: We present the first homomorphically encrypted logistic regression outsourcing model based on the critical observation that the precision loss of classification models is sufficiently small so that the decision plan stays still.

resources.title: Optimized homomorphic encryption solution for secure genome-wide association studies
resources.abstract: Background Genome-Wide Association Studies (GWAS) refer to observational studies of a genome-wide set of genetic variants across many individuals to see if any genetic variants are associated with a certain trait. A typical GWAS analysis of a disease phenotype involves iterative logistic regression of a case/control phenotype on a single-neuclotide polymorphism (SNP) with quantitative covariates. GWAS have been a highly successful approach for identifying genetic-variant associations with many poorly-understood diseases. However, a major limitation of GWAS is the dependence on individual-level genotype/phenotype data and the corresponding privacy concerns. Methods We present a solution for secure GWAS using homomorphic encryption (HE) that keeps all individual data encrypted throughout the association study. Our solution is based on an optimized semi-parallel GWAS compute model, a new Residue-Number-System (RNS) variant of the Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song (CKKS) HE scheme, novel techniques to switch between data encodings, and more than a dozen crypto-engineering optimizations. Results Our prototype can perform the full GWAS computation for 1,000 individuals, 131,071 SNPs, and 3 covariates in about 10 minutes on a modern server computing node (with 28 cores). Our solution for a smaller dataset was awarded co-first place in iDASH’18 Track 2: “Secure Parallel Genome Wide Association Studies using HE”. Conclusions Many of the HE optimizations presented in our paper are general-purpose, and can be used in solving challenging problems with large datasets in other application domains.

sample_claims.text: The cloud provider processes the hospital's patient records only in encrypted form and holds no key that can decrypt them
Individual-level genotype data stay encrypted at every stage on the analysis server, and only the aggregate association statistics are ever decrypted
A breach of the third-party hosting environment exposes only ciphertexts of the bank's customer data, because the secret key never leaves the bank
Encrypted queries sent to the hosted model reveal neither the client's inputs nor the predictions to the operator, even to an administrator with full access to the server's memory and storage

techniques.name: Trigger-Set Model Watermarking
techniques.description: Trigger-set model watermarking lets the owner of a trained classifier show later that a suspect model was copied from theirs, by planting a secret behaviour that only the owner can demonstrate. Before release, the owner chooses a small secret trigger set (in the originating scheme, 100 abstract images), gives each input an arbitrary label unrelated to its content, and trains or fine-tunes the model to return those labels while keeping its accuracy on the real task. In the originating scheme the owner also records cryptographic commitments to the trigger inputs and their labels, which fix the watermark at release so that a trigger set cannot be invented once a dispute has begun. To verify, the owner, or an arbiter shown the opened commitments, sends the trigger inputs to the suspect model through its ordinary prediction interface and counts how many return the assigned labels; an independently trained model matches them at about chance level, so a match rate above a preset threshold is evidence of copying. The technique produces the watermarked model, the commitments and, for each verification, the suspect model's trigger-set accuracy against the threshold.

example_use_cases.description: A medical-imaging company that licenses a chest X-ray classifier for installation on hospital servers, where the weights leave its control, embeds a trigger set before each release and lodges the commitments with a timestamping service. When a near-identical model appears in a rival's product, it queries that product with the trigger images to decide whether there is enough evidence to pursue a licence breach.

Before relying on the watermark in its licence terms, the security team of a retailer that licenses a visual product-search model to partner stores to run on their own servers runs the fine-tuning and pruning attacks in its threat model against the watermarked model, and reports the trigger-set accuracy that survives each, to set the verification threshold and state what the watermark can and cannot evidence.

In a licensing dispute over a satellite-imagery land-use classifier used by a local authority, the developer opens its pre-release commitments to an independent expert, who queries the disputed model's prediction service with the trigger images and reports the match rate against a threshold agreed in advance, without either party handing over model weights.

limitations.description: Removal attacks defeat it in practice. A systematic evaluation of published schemes, trigger-set schemes among them, found none robust against adaptive removal attacks or known ways of deriving a surrogate model, and in the originating paper re-training all layers sharply reduced trigger-set accuracy in models watermarked by fine-tuning. A failed verification does not show a model was not copied, and a robustness claim holds only for the attacks tested.

It evidences copying of the model, not theft through its prediction interface, and needs query access to the suspect. A copy trained on the deployed model's answers (model extraction or distillation) need never see the trigger inputs, and a systematic evaluation found these schemes fail against such surrogates, so extraction needs other defences. A copy used only inside its owner's organisation, or not exposed to queries, cannot be tested at all.

Verification reveals the secret. Sending trigger inputs to a suspect's interface, or showing them to an arbiter, exposes them; an adversary who learns them can fine-tune them away or filter those queries, so verification is in effect single-use unless several trigger sets were embedded or a zero-knowledge protocol is used, both of which the originating paper describes and both of which add work.

Without commitments lodged before release the evidence is weak: whoever holds a copy can embed a second trigger set of their own and claim ownership. In the originating paper's experiments the second set was much less durable under fine-tuning than the first, but that helps only an owner who can show its commitments existed before the disputed model did.

The scheme and its evaluations cover image classifiers that the owner can train or fine-tune with access to the training data. Generative and language models need different designs, and the threshold must reflect the number of classes: an unwatermarked model matched 7.0% of trigger labels on 10-class CIFAR-10 but 1.0% on 100-class CIFAR-100, so chance agreement is far higher with few classes.

resources.title: Protecting Intellectual Property of Deep Neural Networks with Watermarking
resources.abstract: Deep learning technologies, which are the key components of state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence (AI) services, have shown great success in providing human-level capabilities for a variety of tasks, such as visual analysis, speech recognition, and natural language processing and etc. Building a production-level deep learning model is a non-trivial task, which requires a large amount of training data, powerful computing resources, and human expertises. Therefore, illegitimate reproducing, distribution, and the derivation of proprietary deep learning models can lead to copyright infringement and economic harm to model creators. Therefore, it is essential to devise a technique to protect the intellectual property of deep learning models and enable external verification of the model ownership. In this paper, we generalize the "digital watermarking'' concept from multimedia ownership verification to deep neural network (DNNs) models. We investigate three DNN-applicable watermark generation algorithms, propose a watermark implanting approach to infuse watermark into deep learning models, and design a remote verification mechanism to determine the model ownership. By extending the intrinsic generalization and memorization capabilities of deep neural networks, we enable the models to learn specially crafted watermarks at training and activate with pre-specified predictions when observing the watermark patterns at inference. We evaluate our approach with two image recognition benchmark datasets. Our framework accurately (100%) and quickly verifies the ownership of all the remotely deployed deep learning models without affecting the model accuracy for normal input data. In addition, the embedded watermarks in DNN models are robust and resilient to different counter-watermark mechanisms, such as fine-tuning, parameter pruning, and model inversion attacks.

resources.title: Turning Your Weakness Into a Strength: Watermarking Deep Neural Networks by Backdooring
WatermarkNN (PyTorch implementation of Adi et al. 2018)
SoK: How Robust is Image Classification Deep Neural Network Watermarking?
resources.abstract: Deep Neural Network (DNN) watermarking is a method for provenance verification of DNN models. Watermarking should be robust against watermark removal attacks that derive a surrogate model that evades provenance verification. Many watermarking schemes that claim robustness have been proposed, but their robustness is only validated in isolation against a relatively small set of attacks. There is no systematic, empirical evaluation of these claims against a common, comprehensive set of removal attacks. This uncertainty about a watermarking scheme’s robustness causes difficulty to trust their deployment in practice. In this paper, we evaluate whether recently proposed watermarking schemes that claim robustness are robust against a large set of removal attacks. We survey methods from the literature that (i) are known removal attacks, (ii) derive surrogate models but have not been evaluated as removal attacks, and (iii) novel removal attacks. Weight shifting and smooth retraining are novel removal attacks adapted to the DNN watermarking schemes surveyed in this paper. We propose taxonomies for watermarking schemes and removal attacks. Our empirical evaluation includes an ablation study over sets of parameters for each attack and watermarking scheme on the image classification datasets CIFAR-10 and ImageNet. Surprisingly, our study shows that none of the surveyed watermarking schemes is robust in practice. We find that schemes fail to withstand adaptive attacks and known methods for deriving surrogate models that have not been evaluated as removal attacks. This points to intrinsic flaws in how robustness is currently evaluated. Our evaluation includes a discussion of the runtime of each attack to underpin their practical relevance. While none of the schemes is robust against all attacks, none of the attacks removes all watermarks. We show that attacks can be combined and find combined attacks that remove all watermarks. We show that watermarking schemes need to be evaluated against a more extensive set of removal attacks with a more realistic adversary model. Our source code and a complete dataset of evaluation results are publicly available, which allows to independently verify our conclusions.

sample_claims.text: The released model carries a trigger-set watermark whose trigger inputs and labels were committed to, and the commitments lodged, before release
Embedding the watermark reduced the diagnostic model's test accuracy by no more than the tolerance agreed with the clinical safety team
The watermark remained verifiable above the decision threshold after each fine-tuning and pruning attack in the stated threat model
Models trained independently on the same task matched the trigger labels at no more than chance level, giving the verification threshold a measured margin against false ownership claims
Ownership of the licensed model can be demonstrated to an independent arbiter through prediction queries alone, without disclosing either party's model weights

techniques.name: Model Signing
techniques.description: Model signing lets the publisher of a machine-learning model attach a cryptographic signature to the model's files, so that anyone who later loads them can check who released them and that no file has changed since. Under the Open Source Security Foundation's Model Signing (OMS) specification and its reference tool, model-signing, the publisher computes a hash (a short fingerprint that changes if a single byte of the file changes) of every file in the model directory, such as weights, configuration, tokeniser and any dataset files kept with them, lists the hashes in a sorted manifest and signs the manifest, producing a detached signature file kept beside the model. The signature can be made with the publisher's own key, with a certificate from an organisation's certificate authority, or through Sigstore, which issues a short-lived certificate tied to a verified online identity, such as a person's account or a build pipeline's, and records each signing event in a transparency log, an append-only record that can be inspected afterwards. Before loading, the consumer verifies the signature against the signer it expects, recomputes every hash and rejects the model if any listed file differs or is missing or, unless that check is switched off, an unlisted file has appeared, so the evidence is a pass or fail tied to a named signer and an exact set of files. Unlike the unsigned file hashes kept by data-versioning tools, it shows who stands behind the files, and unlike a watermark, which is trained into the weights so that it survives in an altered copy, it is broken by any change; it says nothing about how the model behaves or what it was trained on.

example_use_cases.description: A bank's machine-learning platform team signs each model at the end of its training pipeline, using the pipeline's own workload identity through Sigstore, and configures its model-serving cluster to load only models whose signature verifies against that identity. Its security team watches the transparency log for signing events under that identity that match no approved release, to decide whether a model reached production outside the release process.

A vehicle maker's perception team downloads a pretrained object detector from a supplier catalogue that signs every model it publishes. Before fine-tuning, it verifies the download against the supplier's published certificate and files the verification output in its supplier-acceptance record, so later reviews can show exactly which files the work started from.

A hospital's imaging department receives quarterly updates to a vendor's chest X-ray triage model. Its clinical engineering team verifies each update against the vendor's certificate and rejects any update whose signature fails, or that contains a file the signature does not cover, before it enters the clinical validation environment.

A public research institute releases an open model together with the test set behind its published benchmark, signing both in one bundle, so that a laboratory re-running the benchmark can confirm that the weights and the test data are byte for byte the ones the institute released before comparing its results with the published ones.

limitations.description: It shows who released the files and that they have not changed, nothing more. A model carrying a malicious pickle payload, a backdoor or the effects of poisoned training data verifies perfectly if its publisher signed it, whether through carelessness or because the publisher's own pipeline was compromised before signing. The originating paper states that signing tells the user nothing about what a model does or how it was produced, so content checks are still needed.

A valid signature is only as good as the consumer's check of who made it. A model signed with an attacker's own identity, or by an account named to look like a well-known organisation (a documented attack on model hubs), verifies cleanly unless the verifier insists on the specific identity, certificate or public key it expects. Consumers need a maintained list of trusted signers for each model source.

A stolen signing key, or a compromised account at the identity provider used for Sigstore signing, produces valid signatures. With Sigstore every signature is recorded in a transparency log, so a publisher that monitors the log for its own identity can spot signatures it did not make; with the key and certificate methods the specification does not require a log entry, so misuse of a key may go unnoticed.

Any change to the files breaks verification, including legitimate ones such as quantisation, conversion to another file format or adding a file. Each derived model needs a new signature from whoever produced it, and that signature says nothing about how the derivative relates to the signed original; recording that relationship needs a separate provenance record, such as the pedigree section of an ML-BOM.

It protects only where verification is enforced. Most models on public hubs are unsigned (fewer than 2% of Hugging Face models used the hub's GPG commit-signing option, per studies the originating paper cites), and an unchecked signature protects nobody. Verification re-hashes every file, and hashing dominates the cost: a 1 TB file took about 13 minutes on a 128-vCPU server in the originating paper's benchmark, which matters if very large models are verified at every load.

resources.title: Position: Machine Learning Models Have a Supply Chain Problem
resources.abstract: Powerful machine learning (ML) models are now readily available online, which creates exciting possibilities for users who lack the deep technical expertise or substantial computing resources needed to develop them. On the other hand, this type of open ecosystem comes with many risks. In this paper, we argue that the current ecosystem for open ML models contains significant supply-chain risks, some of which have been exploited already in real attacks. These include an attacker replacing a model with something malicious (e.g., malware), or a model being trained using a vulnerable version of a framework or on restricted or poisoned data. We then explore how Sigstore, a solution designed to bring transparency to open-source software supply chains, can be used to bring transparency to open ML models, in terms of enabling model publishers to sign their models and prove properties about the datasets they use.
